gloss_terse: To solemnly testify, bear witness, or earnestly affirm; to call others to witness the truth of what one declares.
gloss_readable: A verb of solemn public testimony, used when the speaker stakes personal credibility on the truth of a declaration. Paul employs it at critical moments: defending his ministry before the Ephesian elders (Acts 20:26), affirming his gospel before Agrippa (Acts 26:22), and urging the Galatians and Ephesians to grasp the weight of his words. The Spanish 'testifico' and German 'bezeugen' both capture this courtroom gravity. More than casual speech, this is truth-telling with one's reputation on the line.

senses.1: To solemnly testify or earnestly affirm, calling God or others as witnesses to the veracity of one's statement. Paul uses this when the stakes are highest: declaring himself innocent of all blood (Acts 20:26), affirming that every person who accepts circumcision is bound to the whole law (Gal 5:3), and urging believers to walk worthy of God (1 Thess 2:12). The English 'I testify' and French 'attester' both underscore the formal, almost juridical weight of this word.

gloss_terse: Matthew, one of the twelve apostles, formerly a tax collector; also called Levi.
gloss_readable: The personal name of one of Jesus' twelve apostles, a tax collector called from his booth to follow Christ (Matt 9:9). The Semitic form behind the Greek suggests 'gift of God.' French renders him 'Matthieu,' while Spanish and German preserve forms closer to the Greek. He appears in every apostolic list (Matt 10:3, Mark 3:18, Luke 6:15, Acts 1:13) and is traditionally identified with Levi son of Alphaeus, linking the call narratives of Matthew and Mark.

senses.1: The proper name Matthew (Maththaios), designating one of Jesus' twelve apostles. Called directly from his tax-collection post (Matt 9:9), he exemplifies radical discipleship. The name likely derives from Hebrew mattanyah ('gift of YHWH'). Listed among the Twelve in every synoptic catalogue and in Acts 1:13, he is consistently paired with Thomas in the apostolic lists.

gloss_terse: To remove, transfer, or displace from one position or state to another; to cause to change allegiance or location.
gloss_readable: Carries the force of a decisive relocation, whether political, spiritual, or physical. God removed Saul and raised up David (Acts 13:22); the Father transferred believers from the domain of darkness into the kingdom of the Son (Col 1:13). Paul says faith could 'remove' mountains (1 Cor 13:2). The Spanish 'ha apartado' and French 'déplacer' both highlight this sense of authoritative displacement. It implies not merely motion but a change of regime or condition.

senses.1: To remove, transfer, or displace someone or something from one position, authority, or state to another. The word implies purposeful, often authoritative relocation. God 'removed' Saul as king (Acts 13:22); believers are 'transferred' from darkness to Christ's kingdom (Col 1:13); faith could 'remove' mountains (1 Cor 13:2). In Luke 16:4 the steward fears being 'removed' from his post. The German 'versetzen' captures this sense of deliberate repositioning.

gloss_terse: A share, portion, or allotted part; also a district or region; used of one's lot in an inheritance or relationship.
gloss_readable: Denotes a portion that has been apportioned or belongs to someone by right. Mary chose the good 'portion' (Luke 10:42); believers share in the 'inheritance' of the saints in light (Col 1:12). It can also mean a geographical district, as in Acts 16:12 describing Philippi as a leading city of that 'district' of Macedonia. Spanish uses both 'parte' and 'porción,' reflecting the dual sense of allocated share and regional division. Paul asks what 'portion' a believer has with an unbeliever (2 Cor 6:15), extending the word into relational partnership.

senses.1: A share, portion, or allotted part, whether material, spiritual, or relational. Encompasses Mary's choice of the good 'portion' at Jesus' feet (Luke 10:42), the saints' share in the inheritance of light (Col 1:12), and the rhetorical question about what 'share' Christ has with Belial (2 Cor 6:15). Also extends to a geographical district (Acts 16:12). The French 'part' and Spanish 'porción' both reflect the core idea of something apportioned or allotted to a person.

gloss_terse: To share with, give a portion of what one has, or impart generously to another.
gloss_readable: Goes beyond simple giving to emphasize sharing from what one already possesses. John the Baptist urged those with two tunics to 'share' with the one who has none (Luke 3:11). Paul longed to 'impart' a spiritual gift to the Romans (Rom 1:11) and describes sharing not only the gospel but 'our own selves' with the Thessalonians (1 Thess 2:8). The Spanish 'compartir' and German 'mitteilen' beautifully capture this participatory generosity: not giving away everything, but letting others into what you have.

senses.1: To give a share of what one possesses, to impart or distribute generously. The emphasis falls on participatory giving rather than total transfer. John the Baptist commands sharing clothing with those in need (Luke 3:11); Paul desires to impart a spiritual gift (Rom 1:11); the generous person is called to share with zeal (Rom 12:8); the thief must now labor so as to have something to share (Eph 4:28). The Spanish 'compartir' and French 'donner' together highlight the relational warmth of this giving.

gloss_terse: To change outward form or appearance; to transform, disguise, or apply figuratively.
gloss_readable: Focuses on alteration of external form rather than inner nature. Paul 'applied' (transferred as a figure) certain truths to himself and Apollos for the Corinthians' sake (1 Cor 4:6). Satan 'disguises himself' as an angel of light (2 Cor 11:14), and his servants likewise masquerade as servants of righteousness (2 Cor 11:13, 15). Yet the same word describes Christ's power to 'transform' believers' humble bodies into glory (Phil 3:21). Spanish captures both poles: 'apliqué' for the figurative transfer and 'se disfraza' for the deceptive masquerade.

senses.1: To change outward form, disguise, or apply figuratively. Covers a wide range from rhetorical figure (1 Cor 4:6, where Paul 'applied' things to himself as an illustration) to deceptive masquerade (2 Cor 11:13-15, where false apostles and Satan 'disguise' themselves) to eschatological transformation (Phil 3:21, where Christ will 'transform' our lowly bodies). The German 'sich verwandeln' and French 'se déguiser' together capture this spectrum from disguise to genuine metamorphosis.

gloss_terse: To defile, stain, or make ceremonially or morally unclean; to pollute or corrupt.
gloss_readable: Evokes both ritual and moral contamination. The Jewish leaders refused to enter the Praetorium lest they 'be defiled' before Passover (John 18:28), illustrating its ceremonial force. But Paul transforms the concept: to the pure all things are pure, yet to the defiled nothing is pure (Titus 1:15). Hebrews warns against any root of bitterness that might 'defile' many (Heb 12:15), and Jude condemns those who 'defile' the flesh (Jude 1:8). The Spanish 'contaminan' and French 'souiller' both carry the visceral sense of staining something once clean.

senses.1: To defile, stain, or render unclean, whether in ceremonial, moral, or spiritual terms. The Jewish authorities avoid the Praetorium to prevent ritual defilement before Passover (John 18:28). Paul extends the concept inward: the defiled mind and conscience render everything impure (Titus 1:15). The writer of Hebrews warns against a root of bitterness that defiles the community (Heb 12:15), and Jude denounces dreamers who defile the flesh (Jude 1:8). The German 'beflecken' (to stain, besmirch) captures the visceral image of moral pollution.

gloss_terse: To commit adultery; used of both men and women who break the marriage covenant through sexual unfaithfulness.
gloss_readable: A form closely related to moicheuo but appearing in Jesus' teaching on divorce and remarriage. In the Sermon on the Mount and the later dialogue on divorce, Jesus declares that whoever divorces and remarries 'commits adultery,' applying this equally to husbands (Matt 5:32, 19:9; Mark 10:11) and wives (Mark 10:12). Every language surveyed translates with the same direct phrase: Spanish 'comete adulterio,' French 'commettre l'adultere,' German 'Ehebruch begehen.' The word carries unambiguous moral weight, naming the violation of the marriage covenant.

senses.1: To commit adultery, specifically in the context of unlawful remarriage after divorce. Jesus uses this verb to declare that a man who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery (Matt 19:9, Mark 10:11), and likewise a woman who does the same (Mark 10:12). In Matt 5:32 the wrongfully divorced woman is said to be caused to commit adultery. The uniform translation across languages — Spanish 'comete adulterio,' French 'commettre l'adultere' — reflects the directness and gravity of the term.

gloss_terse: A myth, fable, or fictitious story; in the NT, always used negatively for false religious narratives opposed to sound doctrine.
gloss_readable: In classical Greek, mythos simply meant 'word' or 'story,' but by the time of the Pastoral Epistles it had acquired a distinctly pejorative edge. Paul warns Timothy against 'myths and endless genealogies' (1 Tim 1:4), contrasts godly training with 'profane old wives' myths' (1 Tim 4:7), and predicts people will 'turn aside to myths' rather than endure sound teaching (2 Tim 4:4). Titus must rebuke those devoted to 'Jewish myths' (Titus 1:14). Peter insists the apostles did not follow 'cleverly devised myths' (2 Pet 1:16). The German 'Fabel' and Spanish 'mitos' both capture this sense of fabricated, misleading narrative.

senses.1: A myth, fable, or fictitious religious narrative, always used negatively in the NT to describe false teachings that distract from sound doctrine. Paul opposes myths to the truth of the gospel (1 Tim 1:4, 4:7; 2 Tim 4:4; Titus 1:14), and Peter emphatically distances apostolic witness from 'cleverly devised myths' (2 Pet 1:16). The consistent translation across languages — Spanish 'mitos,' German 'Fabel,' French approximating 'fables' — underscores the universally recognized sense of fabricated, misleading stories.

gloss_terse: A mill or millstone; a heavy stone used for grinding grain, often symbolic of catastrophic judgment.
gloss_readable: Refers to both the grinding apparatus and the stone itself. Jesus invokes the millstone in a vivid warning: it would be better to have a great millstone hung around one's neck and be cast into the sea than to cause a little one to stumble (Matt 18:6, Mark 9:42). In the apocalyptic vision, a mighty angel hurls a stone 'like a great millstone' into the sea to dramatize Babylon's fall, and the sound of the mill is heard no more (Rev 18:21-22). Spanish distinguishes 'piedra de molino' (millstone) from 'molino' (mill), reflecting both the object and the place. The everyday domestic item becomes a powerful image of divine judgment.

senses.1: A mill or millstone used for grinding grain, employed both literally and as a dramatic symbol of catastrophic judgment. Jesus warns that causing a child to stumble warrants drowning with a millstone around the neck (Matt 18:6, Mark 9:42). In Matt 24:41, two women grinding at the mill illustrates the suddenness of the coming separation. In Revelation, the angel's casting of a millstone-like boulder into the sea symbolizes Babylon's irreversible destruction, and the ceasing of the mill's sound signifies total desolation (Rev 18:21-22). Spanish 'piedra de molino' and German 'Muehlstein' both preserve the concreteness of this grinding stone.
